extracted.intended_audience: readers of literary biography; scholars and students of Coleridge and Romantic-era literature
extracted.subtask_description: Excerpt from a biographical supplement on S. T. Coleridge containing letters, travel-notes, critical remarks on poetry, and a prospectus for a proposed periodical. Relevant for literary-history context and aesthetic commentaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial scope and format of The Watchman
rubrics_metrics.description: Prospectus: 'This Miscellany will be comprised in two sheets, or thirty-two pages, closely printed in 6vo; the type, long primer. Its contents, 1. A history of the domestic and foreign policy of preceding days. 2. The speeches in both Houses of Parliament; and during the recess, select parliamentary speeches from the commencement of the reign of Charles I. to the present time, with notes historical and biographical. 3. Original essays and poetry. 4. Review of interesting and important publications.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge's plan sets explicit content sections and a compact, regular format; intended advantages listed (bindable annual register, preference for original matter, less abridged parliamentary speeches). Use of a fixed, small format and clearly enumerated sections functions as a production standard for a periodical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid advertisements to prioritise original matter
rubrics_metrics.description: From the prospectus: 'There being no advertisements, a greater quantity of original matter will be given, and the speeches in Parliament will be less abridged.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial decision: omit ads to allocate more space to original writing and fuller reporting. This is an explicit policy criterion for producing an intellectually substantial miscellany rather than an advertising vehicle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the publication bindable and lasting (annual-register aim)
rubrics_metrics.description: From the prospectus: 'From its form it may be bound up at the end of a year, and become an Annual Register. This last circumstance may induce men of letters to prefer this Miscellany to more perishable publications as the vehicle of their effusions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design periodicals with long-term value in mind (format, content selection) to attract contributions and readership seeking permanence; an operational criterion for layout and editorial curation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial neutrality/transparency on conflicting accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: From the prospectus: 'Whenever the Ministerial and Opposition prints differ in their accounts of occurrences, &c., such difference will always be forthwith stated.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When differing accounts of the same event exist, publish both and note the discrepancy promptly. This is an explicit standard for fair reporting and transparency in political/intellectual journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose publication cadence suited to capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Coleridge's judgment: 'To publish a Magazine for one year would be nonsense... It is a thing of monthly anxiety and quotidian bustle.' He therefore proposes a weekly miscellany (The Watchman) as his chosen form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match the frequency of publication to the editor's practical ability and project goals; avoid committing to cadences that create unsustainable workload or reduce quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve the integrity of a poet's text (avoid unnecessary omissions/alterations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical remark: 'Every omission and every alteration disgusted taste, and mangled sensibility.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editing or reprinting a poet's work should avoid arbitrary omissions or changes that harm aesthetic effect or the poet's sensibility; handling of variants should respect original tone and texture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities to value in poetry (as applied to Bowles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Coleridge's appraisal of Bowles: '...descriptive, dignified, tender, sublime. The sonnets added are exquisite. Abba Thule has marked beauties, and the little poem at Southampton is a diamond; in whatever light you place it, it reflects beauty and splendor.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing lyric or descriptive poetry, attend to descriptiveness, dignity, tenderness, sublimity, concentrated excellence in sonnet form, and small poems functioning like 'diamonds' — i.e., compact pieces with high craft and resonance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of framing and distance in landscape description (picturesque principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetic observation: 'A beautiful prospect is always more picturesque when seen at some little distance through an arch.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compositional principle for landscape description: use framing devices (arches, openings) and selective distance to heighten the picturesque effect of a scene; physical frames can increase pictorial interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concealment as a technique to stimulate imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation in travel-note: 'Concealment sets the imagination a-working, and as it were catharactises our desires.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In depiction of sensual or potentially provocative subjects, suggestiveness and partial concealment can be more evocative than explicitness; leaving space for the reader's imagination intensifies emotional or erotic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical balance in political lectures
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical summary of Coleridge's lectures: 'The tone throughout them all is vehemently hostile to the policy of the great minister of that day; but it is equally opposed to the spirit and maxims of Jacobinism.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political rhetoric can take a firm oppositional stance toward specific policies while avoiding alignment with extreme or uncompromising doctrines; balance and discrimination in targets is a rhetorical standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scriptural interpretation must meet standards of sound criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Coleridge on Unitarians: 'I always told the Unitarians that their interpretations of the Scripture were intolerable upon any principles of sound criticism.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretations of authoritative texts (here, Scripture) should conform to principles of sound critical method; strained or intolerable readings are unacceptable within critical discourse.
